conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’m glad you’re here.

Today I’d like to complete a short screening tool called the EPDS—this stands for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a well-validated questionnaire that looks at how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, including checking for signs of depression, anxiety, and any thoughts of self-harm. The goal is simply to understand how you’re coping in this fourth-trimester period so we can offer the right support if you need it.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within the limits of safety, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through 10 questions together; I’ll ask each one conversationally and jot down your answers so you can speak freely. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Looking back over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has it felt hard to find that spark of joy?

I can still laugh sometimes—my partner will make a little joke about how our baby’s socks keep disappearing in the dryer—but it’s definitely harder than it used to be. I have to remind myself to smile, and a lot of things that would have cracked me up before now feel kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time, yes—I can still laugh, just not as easily as before the baby came.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. Sometimes I plan an outing and then feel kind of “meh” when it actually happens.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, a few times this week. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something at lunch that bothered him through my milk, even though the nurse said it probably wasn’t anything I did. I know it’s not rational, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of nights I’ve lain in bed wide-awake, heart racing, running through all the “what-ifs” about the baby—like whether his breathing sounds normal or if the temperature in the room is exactly right. Nothing specific triggered it; I just couldn’t shut the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It hasn’t been full panic, but once or twice I’ve gotten that sudden tight-chest feeling when the baby cried—like my body jumped to “something awful is happening,” even though I knew he probably just needed a diaper change. It passes quickly, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the laundry and bottles and night feeds just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’m not drowning, but I do end most afternoons thinking, “Wow, I’m really tired,” and wondering how I’ll get through the evening routine.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then lie there replaying every little grunt he made, worrying I’ll sleep through his next wake-up. It’s probably three or four nights a week that I toss and turn for an hour before dozing off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had moments—usually when I’m alone feeding him at 3 a.m.—where I just feel kind of heavy and teary. It’s not all day, but a few times this week I’ve caught myself thinking, “I miss feeling like myself.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I got a little teary-eyed yesterday when I couldn’t get him to nap and felt like I was failing, but it didn’t turn into full crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared how, over the past week, laughter and excitement feel muted, worries about your baby keep you awake, and a heavy or teary mood creeps in during night feeds. You're still coping and bonding with your baby, yet you end most days exhausted, wondering how you'll manage the evening routine.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished enjoyment that falls between "rather less" and "hardly at all" but closer to the former, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple instances of self-blame this week, acknowledging it as irrational, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, unprovoked worries disrupting sleep, aligning with "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained physical panic episodes triggered by baby's cry, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and ends most afternoons exhausted and doubting she can finish the evening, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient denies unhappiness but describes persistent, anxiety-driven insomnia 3-4 nights/week; closest to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>The mother reports recurring moments of sadness/tearfulness several times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: Q1-2 show reduced pleasure, Q3 guilt/self-blame, Q4-5 anxiety/panic, Q6-8 fatigue, sadness, tearfulness, Q7 insomnia. A score ≥14 plus functional impact supports probable depression. <quote>I miss feeling like myself</quote> and <quote>I felt like I was failing</quote> highlight mood and self-esteem disturbance. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation
2. Begin evidence-based treatment options: individual <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or consider <med>sertraline</med> if moderate-severe symptoms persist
3. Arrange practical support: partner/family help with night feeds, household tasks, and daytime rest periods
4. Practice daily self-care: 20-min outdoor walk, balanced meals, hydration; limit caffeine after noon
5. Use 5-minute breathing or mindfulness apps when <sym>panic-like sensations</sym> arise; keep baby monitor volume low to reduce startle
6. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
7. If thoughts of self-harm develop, call 988 (US) or local crisis line immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style self-report, 2–3 wk postpartum

Symptoms endorsed  
- Reduced ability to experience pleasure/humor (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt/blame (Q3)  
- Generalized nocturnal anxiety with racing thoughts (Q4)  
- Brief physiologic panic-like episodes when baby cries (Q5)  
- End-of-day fatigue and sense of being “on top of me” (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia unrelated to infant needs (Q7)  
- Intermittent sadness/tearfulness, usually during night feeds (Q8)  
- No crying spells or self-harm ideation (Q9, Q10)

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate dysphoric mood coupled with prominent postpartum-specific worries; functional impact present (sleep disruption, task overload) yet able to bond with infant and maintain basic self-care.

Risk indicators  
- Sleep disturbance linked to mood (Q7)  
- Recurrent rumination and catastrophizing (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective loss of prior enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Guilt cognitions (Q3)  
- No safety concerns (Q10 negative)

Screening impression  
Elevated scores consistent with possible postpartum depression ± anxiety; does not meet threshold for immediate safety intervention. Recommend formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and psychoeducation/referral for evidence-based counseling and medical follow-up.
